utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom, and I may not forget those just outside the courtroom. Without the help of them, we could not have this trial. First of all, I'd like to give the parties the decision of the Chamber on the motion filed by the Defence, a motion which aimed at excluding the evidence of Mr. Deronjic and subsidiary to postpone his testimony until after Mr. Deronjic would have been sentenced. The Chamber has understood that the first part of the motion has been withdrawn, that the Defence did not insist on that any more, so therefore, I'll confirm myself that the Chamber has confined itself to the second part of the motion. The Chamber will deliver its reasoning in writing at a later stage, and it's that reasoning written down on paper that is authoritative. But nevertheless, I'd like to give the parties just a short insight on what moved the Chamber to take this decision. The Chamber, first of all, is aware of the existence of a plea agreement, has studied it, and also the factual statement attached to it. The Chamber, as a matter of principle, expects any witness to take the solemn declaration he gives very seriously. The Chamber has found no legal impediments to hear Mr. Deronjic's testimony prior to a sentence imposed upon him. The Chamber is aware -- the Chamber expects Mr. Deronjic will meet his commitment as we find it in the plea agreement by testifying in accordance with the truth. The Chamber is also aware that the witness who has not been sentenced yet may misinterpret his commitment and might be tempted to give testimony that is influenced by desire to please the Prosecution in order to ameliorate his position in the sentencing proceedings. The Chamber has also considered that Mr. Deronjic will certainly be aware of the risk that any answer given which is not in full accordance with the truth potentially may have a drawback effect on those same proceedings and thus this awareness forms an incitement not to deviate from the truth. The Chamber also considered that the situation before being sentenced and after being sentenced does not create a black-and-white picture. Also, after sentencing, psychological mechanisms might exist that would tempt the witness to adapt his testimony in a way either favourable or unfavourable to the accused. In this case, the trier of fact is a professional Bench, not a jury. Although a professional Bench is not infallible, its professional experience might help a professional Bench to -- not to be misled by any witness, if a witness would intend to mislead the Chamber. The present situation certainly causes the Chamber to very cautiously evaluate whatever evidence will be given. For example, the Chamber will be more focussed on any corroboration by other evidence. And finally, the Chamber will take its task to control the examination of this witness with more than usual seriousness. This just gives a glance on the position the Chamber has led to its decision. The Chamber is informed that a person which, as I understand, is a Defence counsel for Mr. Deronjic would like to make an application before Mr. Deronjic will be called. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning, Your Honours. That is correct. May I introduce, before we commence, Mr. Stephen Margetts, who is a member of the Prosecution team. My name is Mark Harmon. Ms. Javier is the case manager once again. I was informed by Mr. Deronjic and his counsel that Mr. Deronjic requested the presence of his counsel during the testimony, and I have conveyed that message to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that counsel for Mr. Deronjic had already taken a seat in this courtroom, but the Chamber considers it appropriate first to hear the application and then to decide whether or not this application will be granted or denied. Madam Usher, the name of counsel is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cvijetic. You may escort Mr. Cvijetic. Good morning. Would you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am attorney at law, Slobodan Cvijetic, Defence counsel for Mr. Deronjic, who will be heard in this trial as the witness. My presence in this hearing today is the result of his right and his expressed will for me to attend the hearing. My job is to intervene solely on legal issues, but not on facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. You say that you are here because, as a consequence of the right of Mr. Deronjic. Could you please indicate where that right is formulated. Where do we find this right expressed in any rule or in any legal --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for starting before you finished. I think in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it says that in the event that an accused is heard as a witness, he is entitled to ask that his counsel attend the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please guide me to the relevant Rule. If any of the other parties could assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a copy of the Rules at this moment, but -- I'm sorry. That right has never been disputed in the previous cases in which he gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, this Chamber will hear your application, and since you indicated that it's in the Rules, the Chamber would like to know where to find it in the Rules. Perhaps, Madam Registrar, if you would have an extra copy of the Rules that you could -- do we have a B/C/S version of the Rules or do you speak or understand any French or English?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can take my bag and I will try to find the relevant Rule. I have all documents of the Tribunal in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may consult your B/C/S version of the Rules. But if any of the parties could guide the Chamber, that would ... Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have leafed the Rules through quickly. In Article 1 of the Statute, and 20, there are rights of the accused listed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Article 21 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has the right not to give self-incriminating testimony, and certain other rights, among them for his counsel to be present during his evidence and to make sure that his rights are not prejudiced at this hearing, among others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Rule 21 sees the position of an accused when he's tried, evidence at that moment being something totally different, the right to not incriminate yourself is expressed in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, where it says that an accused may not take the stand, it's expressed in the Rule where the right is given to an accused, not to a witness but to an accused, to make an unsworn statement on which he cannot be cross-examined? Is there any legal authority you could invoke to just apply the, I would say almost the complete copies of Article 6 of the European Convention of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights to transplant that to the situation of a witness? Is there any legal authority you could present to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I derived this from Article 21 by analogous interpretation. It is true that Article 21 formulates the right of the accused when he testifies in the capacity of a witness. But even in this case when he testifies as a witness, an accused may find himself in a situation where he is asked to give self-incriminating answers because he is still an accused and I can intervene to stop such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, whether you can intervene or not is for the Chamber to decide. I think that as a matter of fact, that Rule 90, under (E), deals with the matter in more detail than Rule 21. And I will not assume that you expected that this Chamber would not be aware of the existence of this Rule, because this Rule does exist, and that we would not take that seriously. The issue is not whether Mr. Deronjic should answer questions that might incriminate himself, but the issue is what your role would be to prevent that happening, because that's how I understand that you view your own role.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour, and I have already fulfilled this role of mine in his testimony to date. I have attended all of the testimony before the different Trial Chambers. This is the fourth time that this is happening. So the protection of his rights is not in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is subject of the conversation we have at this moment. I don't know whether any of the other chambers -- I'm not informed about that -- any ever asked you questions about the existence of a right you claim that exists. Has there been argument on the issue before you appeared and fulfilled the role as you did?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was discussed, and I did receive a warning that I could make interventions exclusively on legal points but not on factual points and not on anything that the accused would testify about. So I did receive instructions from a Trial Chamber when I could intervene. This is the first time that I've been asked to discuss this matter as something that is disputed. This right has never been challenged before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that, but this Chamber has its own responsibility in establishing what rights are, and I may just remind you that your first answer was that the right was explicitly in the Rules, and it is not in the Rules; at least, that has been established by now. Then may I ask you: How do you envisage that you could intervene? What would trigger your intervention? I mean, at what moment and for what reasons you think you could start an intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Amongst other things, at a point in time if my client was asked a question, the answer to which could incriminate him for some new criminal act or for something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How would you know that his answer would incriminate himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't -- I can imagine that in some situations, it would be clear that an answer to a question might incriminate an accused. If a question would be put to Mr. Deronjic whether he ever, during the events discussed, would have killed someone by his own hands, it doesn't need a lot of guessing whether the answer could -- I'm not saying would, but could incriminate him. On the other hand, there might be a lot of other questions for which it's not that clear whether the answer could incriminate the witness. So therefore, of course there will be clear-cut cases, in which cases perhaps the Chamber might not have great hesitations to accept that Rule 90(E) would apply, but there might be other situations in which it might be totally unclear. Having received instructions by other Chambers, what could you advise me? I mean, could it be that you say this will incriminate you? And then again, apart from the clear-cut cases, how would you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would ask the Trial Chamber's instructions on that. I would intervene, and I would ask the Trial Chamber to decide whether such an answer could or could not incriminate my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- that means you would not consult with Mr. Deronjic, but at that moment you would make an application that the Chamber considers whether the answer could incriminate Mr. Deronjic? Is that right? That means --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, amongst other things, it would be that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say: "Amongst other things," what other things do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also meant the clear-cut situations in which I could intervene and which are obvious. So this would only refer to the situation that you have mentioned just now, when perhaps it would not be clear whether the answer would place my client into an unfavourable situation or not, in which case then I would seek guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware that your intervention could be a signal for Mr. Deronjic either to be more cautious in his answers? Are you aware that you could in this way influence the examination of Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would take care that the desire of Mr. Deronjic to testify in this case is not affected. So I would really be careful not to intervene excessively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but even if you intervene not excessively, it nevertheless could have this effect, if only once. Before we continue -- you're standing. If you'd prefer to be seated, please do so. I'd first like to hear the position --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the parties. Mr. Harmon. And may I also ask you to inform the Chamber about what kind of argument has been held prior to a decision to accept Mr. Cvijetic to be present during the testimony of Mr. Deronjic in other cases, and what exactly the Chambers gave as guidance to Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not attended those other hearings where Mr. Deronjic testified in other proceedings, other than his sentencing hearing, in which counsel had a role as an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. That's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I can't give you an answer to that. I can, Your Honour, looking at the Statute, refer Your Honours to Article 22 of the Statute, which, in the second sentence, says -- it deals with the protection of witnesses: "Such protection measures shall include, but shall not be limited to the conduct of in camera proceedings and the protection of the witness's identity." So this particular part of the Statute gives the Court broad discretion in terms of what protective measures it can apply to a given witness in, I would submit, that in a case where a witness is potentially at risk of incriminating himself, this part of the Statute would permit and allow for the presence of counsel, and I think it would complement Rule 90(E) as well. So I just bring that to Your Honour's attention. I'm not taking an advocacy position in this issue. It's just an aid to Your Honours, bring this to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now in the deliberation this Chamber has held, I never heard Rule 22 protective measures of witnesses being explained as to protect the witness against self-incrimination, but rather to protect the witness against negative responses and negative actions taken upon his testimony because of telling the truth, which might not be always applauded by parts of the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour. I've not heard it applied in this way either. But I just bring it to Your Honour's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- like to introduce a novelty in Rule 22. The Chamber has taken note of that. Mr. Stewart for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. First of all, we do submit that imaginative Mr. Harmon's last intervention was, that can't possibly be what 22 is dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think my response was sufficiently clear that it would need a lot of thinking in order to interpret it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So -- but Your Honour, the Defence's position is this: That we don't, in principle, object to Mr. Deronjic's lawyer sitting in Court, and I've indicated that to Mr. Harmon earlier this morning. We'd also suppose, Your Honour, that there is again in principle no difficulty whatever for the Tribunal in giving permission to Mr. Deronjic's lawyer to sit in Court. We suppose that must be part of the general power of Your Honours to control and steer the conduct of these proceedings. So we don't suggest there is any difficulty whatever if Your Honours feel that it is the right thing to allow him to sit in Court, we don't suggest there can be any conceivable obstacle to that. The Tribunal must have the general power to allow any party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just respond to that very briefly. This Chamber, otherwise we wouldn't hear even any argument on it if we thought we would not have the power to allow Mr. Cvijetic to be in Court, and sitting in Court is one issue, but as you may have noticed, the focus of my questions was mainly on what type of intervention, what role. Just sitting is not the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm coming to that, Your Honour. Because presumably he's sitting here for some purpose after all. If he's simply sitting in court to be an observer, he can sit outside Court and be an observer. So I'm just clearing that particular point out of the way. So far as -- we submit, with respect, that the right course is to have clear ground rules for Mr. Deronjic's lawyer's attendance in Court and we suggest the following: That, first of all, all subject to this, and Your Honour asked the -- asked Mr. Deronjic's lawyer just now: Well, was he aware that his interventions might constitute a signal to Mr. Deronjic? We would suggest that whatever ground rules are indicated, that it should all be subject to this: That if at any point it appeared that Mr. Deronjic's lawyer were to abuse his position, then of course the question of his exclusion would immediately arise. Now, I'm not impugning my learned friend who is sitting there by suggesting that that will happen, but that's the principle of the matter. That of course any permission is in a sense provisional and contingent upon it not being abused, and the Tribunal, of course, would have the power to say: "Well, enough is enough. I'm afraid if you're going to do this, then you are going to have to either keep completely quiet or leave the Court." But we certainly would say that Mr. Deronjic's lawyer should have the opportunity of making on Mr. Deronjic's behalf any objection which arises under 90(E), an objection to a statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. Of course that doesn't remove Mr. Deronjic's own right to make that point at any stage in his evidence. It's not superseded or overridden by that. The -- we recognise that 90(E) refers to a statement which might tend to incriminate the witness which we understand to be in line with normal principles and practice, which is that you don't know in advance of the answer being given for sure whether it is going to have that effect. So as Your Honour indicated, you get a clue from the question. Some questions, and Your Honour gave a good illustration, some questions are very clearly going to lead on to incrimination, self-incrimination, whatever answer is given, if they're answered at all. Some questions carry that clear risk. One positive advantage of having Mr. Deronjic's lawyer in Court, which we recognise, is that if he doesn't have his lawyer in Court, then the responsibility falls on the Tribunal. And we're not suggesting that the Tribunal isn't well able to discharge that responsibility, but it is in principle better, we'd suggest. It's a positive reason for him being in Court, subject to proper ground rules. It is actually better if Mr. Deronjic's own lawyer is in a position to make those objections, then the Tribunal doesn't quite have the task, then, on Mr. Deronjic's behalf. Although you wouldn't abrogate that task altogether anyway because it's part of the Chamber's responsibility. The Chamber would have the support of Mr. Deronjic's lawyer in relation to that. And it's all subject to this, then: That provided that the objections were only made properly and professionally and in the light of experience as Mr. Deronjic's evidence proceeds, there was no problem about it, then we'd suggest the Tribunal could continue in that way. If there were any question of abuse, well, we would have to, as we say, cross that bridge when we come to it. We'd simply like to add this, Your Honour, that we do suggest that the ground rules, with respect, Your Honour, we do propose that ground rules are the right approach, that it is limited to that, that when there's any reference to legal submissions, we don't at the moment see any basis on which Mr. Deronjic's lawyer would have any part in any legal submissions or any other aspect of the case and simply the question of objections on Mr. Deronjic's behalf under 90(E). Note one can never say never, as far as unexpected circumstances come up as was recognised yesterday. But as a starting point we should say that that should be the indication, that Mr. Deronjic's lawyer's role would be limited to such objections under 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would there be any suggestion from the Prosecution on what should be ground rules to be adopted by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I submit that the submissions by Defence counsel are entirely appropriate, and I think that is all that needs to be said from the Prosecution on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Cvijetic, would you like to add anything to what you heard the parties have submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, except that I still abide by the application of Article 21 of the Statute, (G), and also we have the Rule of Evidence and Procedure 90(E). I would also like to add that my presence perhaps can contribute to the fulfilment of justice and the credibility and the truthfulness of the testimony of my client when we have in mind that his testimony was given in the presence of his attorney, and I also support what my colleagues have said. I don't have any other arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... very short point is this: That we also suggest -- I should have done this -- that unless with the express permission of the Tribunal there should be absolutely no communication between Mr. Deronjic and his lawyer until he has completely finished giving his evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would accommodate you, Mr. Stewart, I discussed already with the registrar before this hearing that if the Chamber would allow Mr. Cvijetic to be in the courtroom, that he would be in a position where even no eye contact would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, that's an additional protective measure in that context, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Chamber will take a few minutes to consider the matter, and especially we'll also try to do it as quickly, even although novel interpretations of not only Article 21 but Article 22 are suggested. But we'll try to deal with it in a couple of minutes. We adjourn. --- Break taken at 9.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the Chamber delivers a decision on your application, but not after having given some consideration that could guide you, because the decision is in favour of your presence. But the Chamber would like to keep you a few things in mind. The first is that the analysis of the situation, as we heard it here in Court, is deficient. What is the situation? The situation is that Mr. Deronjic has pleaded guilty and that part of the commitment of the Prosecution is that they dropped additional charges, if I well understand, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The charges that are against Mr. Deronjic are the only charges before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were no other charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There were no other charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But then perhaps I need a clarification. May I take it that if Mr. Deronjic fulfils all his obligations under the plea agreement, that no further charges will be brought against him, at least charges related to -- let me just say it very roughly -- Bratunac 1991, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina, joint criminal enterprise, and what happened in the framework of the joint criminal enterprise? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, whatever answer would be given in this context, whether incriminating or not, and that's the basis of the Rule, not to incriminate yourself, is that you would expose yourself to prosecution, is not a real problem unless you would not trust the Prosecution in its commitment. The second possibility is that Mr. Deronjic might reveal details about his own behaviour that might deteriorate his position in the sentencing proceedings. We do understand, however, that Rule 90(E) would protect him against that, because whatever fact may become known that is not part of the factual statement underlying the plea agreement should be proven in sentencing proceedings, and Rule 90(E) could protect him from that. So that is clear. There is another issue, and that is that Rule 90(E) and the plea agreement may give some protection to Mr. Deronjic in this Tribunal, and I saw that even in the plea agreement, there is a clause saying -- I just have to find it. The Prosecution will inform whatever domestic authority that in -- that this plea agreement and sentencing -- I haven't got it. I read it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 11, sub-part (d).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that would at least result in an effort of the Prosecution to prevent any domestic prosecutions to take place at a later stage somewhere else. That's, of course, not a full guarantee. If it would ever come to any detail, so that's not what one could expect in the framework of the public statement of facts, because the plea agreement is a public document, but if it would ever come to any other detail which is outside the scope of that statement of facts, and if Mr. Deronjic would fear that he would be prosecuted for that elsewhere, then he could indicate so, because one of the solutions then might be to go in private session or to go in closed session. I already indicate to you that there's hardly any such risk to be expected from any jurisdiction in the former Yugoslavia, at least if the incrimination would be covered by the Statute of the Tribunal, because the Tribunal has the power to stop whatever prosecutions would be started and either take over the case. So therefore, but if Mr. Deronjic would incriminate himself by saying that he learned to do this or that in Italy or Austria, and if this would incriminate him, then of course there could be a serious need to protect him against such prosecutions by hearing his testimony in private or closed session. So therefore, it should not be too easily invoked that Mr. Deronjic is, by his self-incrimination, would expose himself to prosecutions elsewhere. The Chamber allows you, Mr. Cvijetic, to be present. The Chamber is also aware that there would be hardly any need, presumably, to intervene during the examination-in-chief, because the situations I just described, where there might be a realistic risk of being prosecuted on the basis of the testimony or having to face the consequences in sentencing proceedings where it still has to be proven, and you also have to weigh out to say 90(E) would apply here for sentencing reasons, that it could not be used as evidence against Mr. Deronjic. But that would not be a reason not to answer the question. Mr. Deronjic will be sufficiently protected. Another way of dealing with it would be that if the Prosecution would on from the beginning say that whatever is in his testimony will not be used in addition to what is in the factual statement to be used for submissions in order to impose a more severe sentence to Mr. Deronjic to be used against him in sentencing, then the matter would not arise at all in this respect. I'll ask in a minute to Mr. Harmon what his position would be to that, because it would be -- it would make the examination more smooth. The Chamber, on the basis of the analysis of where the real risks could be, is aware that the chances that any such matter could arise might be greater in cross-examination than examination-in-chief. So, Mr. Cvijetic, you may be present. You may intervene, but you should keep clearly in mind that an answer that could incriminate Mr. Deronjic, in most situations, would have no effect, since he'll not be prosecuted for any facts that are covered, I would say, by the global concept of 1991, 1992, Bratunac, joint criminal enterprise, Bosnia-Herzegovina, in that situation. So therefore, it would not be necessary to intervene, and the Chamber, of course, fully accepts your role on where the real risks are. Then I indicated that I would ask Mr. Harmon whether he could give a general commitment on the use of incriminating testimony for sentencing purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the events in Glogova, we will make that commitment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have a limited commitment as far as Glogova is concerned, which of course is not the only thing, but I can imagine why Mr. Harmon gives this explanation. Is your position clear? And I would add to that that you'll be -- you'll have to be in a position where there's no direct contact with Mr. Deronjic. And as I said, also no eye contact. So I don't know. I'll instruct Mr. Deronjic not to seek any eye contact with you if he will be called. Is this -- I mean, the decision might be quite clear. Is the guidance clear enough for you? And does any of the parties have any questions in respect of the guidance I gave to Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour, the Defence. In fact it's -- well, there's one question that I -- we do have and one submission. May I make the submission first. Your Honour said in delivering the decision just in the last few minutes that, and I'm reading from the transcript, as it stands at the moment: The second possibility -- it's at 10 -- it's line 16 of the previous page, and, well, the time is 10: -- What page is that? It's page 16, line 16. It was at 10:13:33. Page 16, line 16: "The second possibility is that Mr. Deronjic might reveal details about his own behaviour." Do Your Honours see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That passage? "...might reveal details about his own behaviour that might deteriorate his position in the sentencing proceedings. We do understand, however, that Rule 90(E), would protect him against that because whatever fact may become known that's not part of the factual agreement underlying the plea agreement should be proven in sentencing proceedings, and Rule 90(E) could protect him from that." Your Honour, our submission, with respect, is that is simply wrong, with the greatest respect. There is no basis on which Rule 90(E) could possibly protect Mr. Deronjic, and not only that, but it would be exactly contrary to precisely why Mr. Deronjic is giving evidence. He is coming to -- there is -- may we say with the greatest respect, Your Honour, that there's a very considerable danger in this situation that everybody loses track of the fact that the person who is primarily entitled to protection here is Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Deronjic is a subsidiary person, as far as -- he's an important person, of course. He's a witness, and when he gives evidence he's critically important but it is Mr. Krajisnik who is on trial here, and it is Mr. Krajisnik's rights to be protected. And the notion that a witness can refuse to answer anything and should in any way adjust his testimony because that testimony might have a harmful effect on his position in the sentencing proceedings is fundamentally wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. -- let me just interrupt you. I had in mind at that moment, and of course it needs an interpretation of Rule 90(E), that if the Chamber would force the witness to answer the question, that the testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence and then it reads: In subsequent prosecution, and the Chamber then interprets a subsequent prosecution also, a subsequent stage of the pending prosecution of the witness in respect of sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's my point. That's what we say is wrong, that there is a fundamental distinction here, that the -- of course, the Chamber does have the right to insist that he answers the question anyway, and then the answer can't be used, but in -- the Chamber at each case has a discretion to exercise. What we are submitting is that when it is not a question of incrimination but a question of sentencing, that that discretion doesn't even arise in the first place, that it's not -- that Rule 90(E) is not triggered at all, that there is no -- there will be and is no proper basis even for the objection in the first place if the matter is not a question of incrimination, in other words, leading to any additional conviction by any Tribunal in relation to a criminal offence, but if it is simply a question of making his position worse in relation to sentencing, then Rule 90(E) has no application at all, and that is -- our submission is contrary to the passage which I've just cited from Your Honour's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You say 90(E) does not apply under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We do say that, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any observation to be made by the Prosecution in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's none, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not give a decision in more general terms on whether Rule 90(E) would ever apply or would not apply under these circumstances. We'll cross that bridge when we come to that. It might be that there will be no intervention at all. We do not know that yet. Of course, the Chamber hopes not to have given similar, novel interpretation of Rules as the third -- as a third time this morning. It's your submission that Rule 90(E) does not apply in these circumstances. When it comes to that, that means that whenever the witness invites us, or the witness indicates that because of the incriminating answer to be expected, he will not answer a question, when we would decide to force him to answer that question, we have to cross the bridge on whether Rule 90(E) applies, yes or no, and we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Your Honour. The -- in 20 seconds, if the answer might tend to lead truly to incrimination, then Rule 90(E) would apply and Your Honours would then have to exercise your discretion. Our submission in an absolute nutshell is that if it is not a question of potential incrimination but merely making his sentencing position worse, then Rule 90(E) simply has no application at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you it's a matter of interpretation of what incrimination or to incriminate precisely means, whether that is just the -- I would say the technical legal term or whether it could be -- have a more extensive meaning which would also influence. So it's not to start a prosecution but to be of any influence on a prosecution, apart from whether he could be prosecuted for that, whether that would be in this Tribunal, in the present situation, or whether the answer is such that, in general terms, you could expect incrimination -- a prosecution. Let me also say that, as I indicated before, we're not only dealing with the Tribunal, but of course there are other jurisdictions as well. So therefore, do you look at it as an abstract possibility to be prosecuted for it, or do you see it as a real possibility to be prosecuted in this Tribunal? Let's not make this courtroom a debating club, although we highly appreciate the observations you made. The decision has been given. You've made your submissions, and you said you would like to make an observation as well. Or was that already included in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It was a separate matter. So I understand that if this bridge comes for us to cross, that, of course, appropriate submissions would then be in order at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. On that basis then -- the other one was a question, and it's a point that I alluded to earlier, so that there is no room for misunderstanding. It is our request that Mr. Deronjic's lawyer should have, except with the express permission of the Tribunal, should have no communication at all with Mr. Deronjic until Mr. Deronjic has fully completed his evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to you, Mr. -- we have of course I have not dealt in detail with that. First of all, the main reason for your presence is, I would say, the possible incriminating character of any answers of Mr. Deronjic. I think we dealt with that sufficiently now. You may address the Chamber, and you're not supposed to communicate directly with Mr. Deronjic. I'll explain that to him. And there's another issue, and that is that if there would be anything else than this focus point of your presence, you would have to ask leave to address the Chamber, and we might ask Mr. Deronjic to leave the courtroom before you explain what you'd like to submit to the Chamber. If that is clear to you -- do you have any questions or issues -- or is the situation clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I wish to thank you for granting the application of the Defence of Mr. Deronjic to attend this hearing. I think it is a just decision and a fair one, and it will contribute to the fairness of the entire proceedings. We will not open a debate now, because you have already made your decision. I only want to give you my assurances and another point. I am grateful for dealing with this issue at some length, but I want to give you my assurances that there will be no problems arising out of this rule, and I think we can start right now. All the other issues that you have mentioned, including the conduct of Mr. Deronjic and my own conduct during the proceedings, have the other facet, Dominus Litus, and I assure you that everything will be appropriate during this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties asked me yesterday to give a better schedule in the morning when we would have breaks or not. Yesterday I adapted the schedule a bit also to the interruptions we had and the other breaks. As a general rule, you could expect to start with one hour and a half, then have a 20-minute break, then continue for another one hour and 25 minutes, then a quarter of an hour break and then the remaining I think 50 minutes would be the last part. That's the general schedule, but not only yesterday, but also today we, for all kind of unexpected things, the course of events was a bit different. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00, and I'd like then to first have Mr. Deronjic to be brought in, in order to instruct him, and only afterwards, Mr. Cvijetic, you'll be escorted into the courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you'd like to address the Chamber, and I'm not going to say that you should keep it brief, because we've lost a lot of time but because we spent already a lot of time this morning on issues. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I thought Your Honour might say you weren't going to ask me to keep it brief because I always do anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will keep it brief, as I always do. Your Honour, the first point is this: We are troubled in relation to the undertaking which Your Honour mentioned, which has been given by the Prosecution. It in the first place is only limited to Glogova, but we're troubled for this reason, that we do seriously question whether that undertaking is in fact possible to give in any effective form, for this reason, and I made it to clear to Mr. Harmon, I'm net impugning Mr. Harmon's professionalism, but there is the underlying question of whether it can properly be given. It's at page 19, line 10. And the reason why we question the matter is this: That it can only be operative in practice in this way, which is that the material, the evidence given, let's suppose, by Mr. Deronjic in relation to such a matter which would be affected by this undertaking is then withheld from the sentencing Tribunal. Because if it is not withheld from the sentencing Tribunal then, as we understand to be entirely clear, any undertakings, any commitments and any guidance and any recommendations by the Prosecution in relation to sentencing are of course, in principle, always liable to be overridden by the Tribunal in the proper exercise of its discretion and its powers in relation to sentencing. We understand that to be crystal clear. So that on the simplest level a recommendation by the Prosecution as to the appropriate sentence can be, and in at least one case we're aware of has been overridden by a heavier sentence being imposed. So that the undertaking, we'd suggest that the first course, which is that that evidence should be withheld from the sentencing Tribunal, is in principle improper, and it's improper from the point of view of the procedures of the Tribunal, and it's also improper in the broader sense, because Your Honour has alluded to broader issues as opposed to technical, legal issues. But it is an extraordinarily unsatisfactory result, to put it mildly, if the world at large in this public trial hears Mr. Deronjic give some evidence which is clearly capable of having an impact as a matter of common sense on his sentencing in relation to the charges to which he's pleaded guilty, and yet the world at large sees, if it's looking hard enough, but the principle is that the world at large does in some case look hard through the media or whatever. They see that that very material, which has appeared in evidence in this case has then not been put before the Tribunal which is sentencing. And in the over -- the overall interests of justice and the overall aims and principles of this Tribunal, we suggest that's an entirely wrong course. And once the material is -- as we've indicated, once the material is put before the sentencing Tribunal, it cannot possibly be ignored and it has to be given its full weight regardless of any undertakings which have been given by the Prosecution in this specific case. So that there is really a very considerable difficulty with that approach. Your Honour, may I make my second observation, then, or second submission at the same time. Because they're not unrelated. And it is this: That we have -- of course we knew the -- we knew the simple result, if I could call it that, of our motion to defer Mr. Deronjic's evidence until after sentencing. We knew that yesterday afternoon, and it was certainly helpful to us to know that late yesterday afternoon. We don't yet know, of course, the full reasons, but Your Honour has very helpfully given everybody a summary of the essential reasons for the decision. But we have, of course, in the very limited time this morning, we have considered the matter, and we have considered the question of appeal. And we understand that under Rule 73, and we're looking particularly at 73(B), that decisions on all motions are without interlocutory appeal, which this plainly would be, save with certification by the Trial Chamber, which may grant such certification if the decision involves an issue that would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial, and for which, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. And then there's a time limit for request for certification. It's seven days. But of course given what we're dealing with at the moment, Your Honour, it would be quite unrealistic to suppose that anybody should let seven days tick by in this case, which is why we're raising it immediately. Under 73(B), there are the two conditions which have to be satisfied for certification to be granted. One, that it would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. That point has the familiar underlying difficulty that in a sense, it relates, or if you like can pre-empt the result of the appeal. It's clearly the Defence's position that it is an issue that would significantly affect the fair conduct of the proceedings, or is capable of affecting the outcome of the trial. And in effect to say that it wouldn't is essentially to pre-empt the appeal decision. Now, of course, in a case where we acknowledge this, in a case where a Tribunal considers that there is absolutely no doubt whatever about the matter so that an appeal is in effect an abuse or has absolutely no reasonable prospect of success, then in domestic and international tribunals that is exactly the situation in which a Tribunal will and should refuse leave to appeal or refuse certification. But we do say in relation to that matter, but I'm taking it very briefly right now, as Your Honour has invited me to do and also in the light of the fact that of course we have had only a very limited opportunity to consider the summary of reasons that Your Honour has given us. So that's condition number one. Condition number two, which in the opinion of the Trial Chamber an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. Advance the proceedings, again, we're in the realm of interpretation, but it can't mean, we'd suggest it can't mean advance the proceedings in the simple sense of it moves everything along quicker. That couldn't be right, because the essential point is what is fair and what is the right decision, and it's possible to imagine all sorts of decisions where inevitably having an appeal doesn't advance the proceedings in the sense of immediately moving them on more quickly. It must be in effect subsidiary to the essential requirement relating to the fair and expeditious, we acknowledge, but fair conduct of the proceedings is, after all, the underlying aim and the underlying principle. Now, the reason we raise it now, Your Honour, is because clearly, once we start Mr. Deronjic's evidence, the position changes, because if we get at all deeply into Mr. Deronjic's evidence, the position becomes even more satisfactory and in effect, then, any possible outcome of the appeal is pre-empted then by the fact that that's happened because we would end up with a terribly messy combination, if we were in principle otherwise going to be successful on appeal. Mr. Deronjic having given some of his evidence while the objection that the Defence has put forward, and Your Honours have so far ruled against, that objection is a live objection that the sentencing hearing is hanging over him. If the appeal were then hypothetically successful, the rest of his evidence would be deferred until after sentencing and that would be a most unsatisfactory position. We acknowledge that. But the effect is, therefore, that to start Mr. Deronjic's evidence is in effect, in practice, without making a concession on this, but it has a very strong tendency to pre-empt the result of any appeal. Accordingly, Your Honour, at this stage, because we do wish to make that request for certification, but we would wish to have an opportunity of considering a little bit more carefully with time to discuss it and look at it, the reasons that Your Honour has given this morning and to consider whether there are further submissions that we'd want to make on this very important item at this stage. We would invite Your Honours to rule that Mr. Deronjic should not begin his evidence today because for the reasons we've indicated, that once he has begun his evidence the position has changed then immediately in a most unsatisfactory fashion. So we are, Your Honour, at a quarter past 11.00 today, but we would invite Your Honour to make that ruling and to give us, the Defence, the opportunity of making a fully developed submission in relation to this matter, unless of course Your Honour, naturally, if Your Honours were inclined to grant our certification this morning, then naturally that's something that we would willingly accept. But that certification would be of no practical value unless Mr. Deronjic's evidence were deferred for the time being while we took the necessary steps formally to lodge our appeal or to file our appeal and make the necessary arrangements for an Appeal Chamber to hear the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to start the testimony of Mr. Deronjic today. In respect of the events in Glogova, Mr. Deronjic has given an extensive statement about the events in Glogova, a copy of which has been furnished to the Defence a long time ago. He has detailed some of those events in a factual basis, which form the basis of his guilty plea. Thirdly, he has taken the oath and sworn about -- he has taken the oath and given sworn testimony in his sentencing hearing before the Chamber presided over by Judge Schomburg. Judge Schomburg I know is very attentive to these matters. I have no doubt in my mind that Judge Schomburg and that Chamber will be aware of what is in the public record in respect of Mr. Deronjic's testimony about Glogova. In respect of whether or not the application for certification to appeal, our position is this: We think that the matter should be rejected. We think that the matter -- Mr. Deronjic's testimony should proceed today. And we have no additional submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have two issues. The first is the commitment given by Mr. Harmon on Glogova, where you doubt whether it's a right course to take. This does not require a decision, but I just make two observations. The first is that whether or not Mr. Deronjic will testify or not. And that also means whether there's at all any possibility of public exposure of additional elements relevant for sentencing is in the discretion of the Prosecution. And the second observation I'd like to make is that part of the validity of your argument also depends on the applicability of Rule 90(E), which of course has as its effect that sometimes information may be known to the public which could not be used for the reasons on which Rule 90(E) is based to prosecute someone. And if Rule 90(E) applies, the same would be true for the information to be taken into consideration by a sentencing. That is perhaps not the most ideal situation, but it's a reality. Then the second issue, whether we should not start the testimony of Mr. Deronjic. That's a matter I'd like to discuss with the Judges very briefly. I really hope to be back in two or three minutes. It's a -- we have to consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one single observation on something Your Honour has just said. Your Honour just said that whether there was any possibility of public exposure of additional elements to sentencing is in the discretion of the Prosecution. Your Honour, we don't fully understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By calling. It's up to the Prosecution whether they want to call Mr. Deronjic or not, and therefore it's a consequence of the calling of Mr. Deronjic whether in a public hearing any additional information about behaviour of Mr. Deronjic would come to the public, and therefore, whether the public could be upset about this not to be taken into consideration in later proceedings. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes I thank you for that clarification, Your Honour. Because once he's in the witness box then, of course, it's no longer under the control of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said it, the first is whether he will testify or not, and that means -- and it's just calling him as a witness. We'll adjourn for a couple of minutes. --- Break taken at 11.19 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered your application, Mr. Stewart, and the Chamber is aware that your submission necessarily had a kind of a provisional character because you have not received our decision in writing, and there was not much time to think about the matter. Nevertheless, the Chamber has decided to start with the examination of Mr. Deronjic. The Chamber is not convinced, or perhaps I should say not convinced yet, because we're still awaiting, of course, a further written submission in this respect. We're not convinced yet that the second requirement, the material advance of the proceedings, would be fulfilled. For that reason, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I ask a clarification, Your Honour? That Your Honour is in effect saying that we are able in effect to renew the provisional application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I started with. And time has been limited, so if -- I would say if there would have been a prima facie case for your submission, then of course it might have been different, but since we are aware that the short time you had available, the Chamber will not prevent you from submitting in writing any further argument that -- not to start, but then to stop immediately the testimony, the examination of Mr. Deronjic. But the Chamber sees no reason at this moment not to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then that's clear. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like, Madam Usher, the next witness to be brought into the courtroom, and the next witness you call, Mr. Harmon, it might not be a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. It isn't. Miroslav Deronjic. Yes, thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please. He'll be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you're Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Deronjic, you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I'm Miroslav Deronjic, and I understand what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make your solemn declaration, and the text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. Please be seated. Mr. Deronjic, I'd like to give you a few instructions before we start your examination. First of all, your counsel applied for being present and we allow him to be present. But you're instructed not to communicate with counsel. Your counsel knows exactly what we expect him to do and not to do, and what he's supposed not to do is to consult with you but to address the Chamber. This means that you're also instructed not to seek any eye contact with counsel. Just concentrate on those who are examining you and concentrate on the Chamber. That's point one. Second point is: The Chamber is aware that you've entered into a plea agreement. The Chamber is also aware that you're still awaiting to be sentenced. In the plea agreement, but more important, in the solemn declaration you just gave, you declared that you'll speak the truth, nothing but the truth, and the whole truth. In transcripts of public hearings in this Tribunal, we find - and I didn't read any other part than specifically those parts - we find passages in which you testified that earlier statements might, for whatever reasons, not be true. Perhaps not in full, but then at least in part. You then testified that, for reasons that moved you to decide not to give true statements. I hope it's clear to you that no reason whatsoever, also not reasons that might be favourable for you in sentencing, could justify one word not being true. I want you to be aware of that. I also want you to be aware that if you give false testimony in this Court, which of course the Chamber does not expect you to do, that you'd be liable and you could be prosecuted for giving false testimony. Did you understand every single word I said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Cvijetic may be escorted into the courtroom. I do not know for security reasons whether you have to sit at that side. Would it be possible to sit in between the -- is it impossible? I'm just asking. I've got no idea about security regulations. No, no. Just to sit in between the counsel and the witness. THE GUARD: As you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to have a security officer not too small today. Yes. You may escort Mr. Cvijetic into the courtroom. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were born on the 6th of June, 1954, in the Bratunac municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you are a Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges your educational background, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I completed the department of philosophy at the University of Sarajevo, the department for Yugoslav literature, and by occupation, I am professor of the Serbian language and literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges your professional background. What did you do after you graduated from university?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I will try to be brief. After graduating from the university, I worked for a while in a daily newspaper, the republican daily newspaper of Bosnia-Herzegovina, called Oslobodjenje, as revisor, and after that, for a while, I worked in a high school called Igmanski Mars, in Sarajevo, whereafter I found in job in Bratunac. I forgot to say that in that period when I lived in Sarajevo, I continued in post-graduate studies, which I did not complete. Instead I returned to Bratunac. And for a short time, I worked in a high school in Srebrenica, before I went to do my military service. After coming back home, I again worked in the high school in Srebrenica, and after that, I went to France, where I lived for two years, working in a job that involved working with children of Yugoslav guest workers in France. After that contract expired, I again took up employment in the high school in Srebrenica, where I remained until the beginning of the war. In the summer of 1990, I was elected president of the SDS in Bratunac, in which post I remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, you're currently awaiting sentence before this Tribunal, having entered a plea of guilty to a single count of persecutions in relation to your role in events in Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my first exhibit is going to be a copy of the plea agreement that was entered into with the Prosecution's -- Prosecutor's office on the 29th of September, 2003, a copy of the second amended indictment, and the factual basis that supports that guilty plea. If I could have the exhibit number on that, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P33.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I won't ask you any additional questions in respect of that particular --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will not ask you any additional questions in respect of Prosecutor's Exhibit P33. Let me -- Mr. Deronjic, let me take you to another set of exhibits. Since your testimony will principally deal with events that took place in the Bratunac municipality, in order to assist the Trial Chamber, I have prepared two exhibits. If I could have these two exhibits marked next in order. One -- I'll give these to the usher. The first exhibit is -- would be in order would be the map with the Bratunac municipality highlighted, right-hand corner. What is the exhibit number on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P34. And the next map will be Exhibit number P35.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, on the screen in front of you is a map. Does that map accurately reflect the location of the Bratunac municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the accurate position of Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the Bratunac municipality borders with Serbia on what would be the right-hand side of this map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could -- Exhibit P35. Mr. Deronjic, this is a map showing not only the Bratunac municipality, but a number of municipalities in Eastern Bosnia. Do you recognise this as such?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Harmon. I recognise the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you see a scale on the bottom left-hand corner of this map?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to give the Judges some perspective about the size of this area. Could you tell the Judges, in terms of the location of the Srebrenica municipality, how far away is the Srebrenica municipality by car, travelling at a normal rate of speed, from the town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Town to town, it's ten kilometres, which means about a ten-minute ride by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, focussing your attention on the city of Zvornik, in the Zvornik municipality, again, from the town of Bratunac to the town of Zvornik - Zvornik is indicated above Bratunac - how long would it take you to travel between those two cities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Half an hour. These two towns are 43 kilometres away from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Moving north to Bijeljina, I pose the same question to you, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: An hour's ride, because Bijeljina is exactly 100 metres away from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. So I won't take you through the remaining points on this particular map, Mr. Deronjic, but suffice it to say, would you agree with me that the distances between the Bratunac municipality and some of the major points about which your testimony will touch upon is not very far?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I completely agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, let me ask you: When did you join the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I joined the SDS party in August 1990, and at that first meeting which I attended, I was elected president of the initiative committee for the founding of the party, and I became president formally on the 2nd September, the date of the founding assembly of the SDS party in Bratunac. I'm speaking of year 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you join the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: There were many reasons, of course. In the period that preceded that, I was not involved in politics. I was not a member of the League of Communists, and in a certain sense, I was dissident, if you could call it that. And I thought it logical and natural that in the period of the dissolution of the League of Communists and the introduction of the multi-party system, I should opt for one of the parties. The SDS was not my first choice at the beginning. For a while, in the beginning, I tried to set up the Serbian renewal movement, together with some friends and colleagues, the intellectuals in Bratunac, but we soon realised that it would be a marginal party and there is no real reason to found it. Whereas the SDS had already been established as a major party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I decided, in agreement with all the people who had been trying earlier to set up a Serbian renewal movement, to join the SDS. And as I said, at the first meeting, I was elected president of the initiative committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to come to that right now, Mr. Deronjic. Could you describe to the Judges what positions you held in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will describe all the positions I held. I was president of the SDS in Bratunac until spring 1996, when I resigned. On the republican level, I was member of the Main Board, starting with 1993, when the SDS resumed its work, because it is a well-known fact that the work of all political parties had been suspended during the war in 1992, under a decision of the then-government of Republika Srpska, and the party therefore resumed its work in the beginning of 1993. I came on to the Main Board to replace Goran Zekic, who was a colleague of mine and who was president of the SDS in Srebrenica. And before me was the main representative on the Main Board for that area. I was co-opted to the Main Board, not elected because there had been no elections. After that, from 1996 to 1997, I was vice-president of the Serb 11 Democratic Party, when the party reformed itself, and instead of an Executive Board, it had a Presidency, consisting of seven vice-presidents. I was one of those elected to the Presidency of the Serbian Democratic Party. In the autumn of 1997, I was elected into the committee for personnel affairs and continued in that position until the committee was 16 abolished, and the competencies of that committee were taken over by the 17 presidency of the Serbian Democratic Party.THE INTERPRETER:Interpreter's 18 correction.The year is 1991, not 7. Answer.I might just add that, as a member of that commission, I do not remember a single meeting of that commission in 20 1991. In 1992,the party did not work and there were no meetings.I think I 21 started to attend the first of those meetings in 1993 when the party resumed 22 its work. I omitted to say maybe that in the period from April--actually, end 23 April to mid-June 1992, I was president of the Crisis Staff in Bratunac 24 municipality.It was a municipal crisis staff.It is also a well-known fact 25 that in autumn 1991,the SDS organised crisis staffs across all the 1 municipalities, and I was president of the Crisis Staff of the Bratunac 2 municipality in that period. 3 MR. HARMON:Q. Could you tell the Judges what your duties and responsibilities were when you were the president of the Bratunac municipal board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I had many duties. It is well known that immediately after the establishment of all these parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, multi-party elections were held. They were the first multi-party elections in our republic. So that we spent the autumn of 1990 mainly preparing for the elections. That involves a lot of work, preparing nominations at municipal and republican level. We had to hold a lot of sessions, rallies, public debates, and those were the activities that occupied our time in 1990. In 1991, we mainly carried out the decisions of 14 republican party organs and Goran Zekic was our link with the republican 15 organs, who became later representative in the Republican Assembly for our 16 area. We also received written instructions on how to conduct our activities 17 in our areas. Later, we were also in charge of implementing election results 18 and dividing positions and competencies in keeping with the election results. 19 We held a series of meetings with the SDA party, which was the majority party 20 in Bratunac. The ratio was 70:30, if my memory serves me well.The SDA won 21 about 70 per cent of the votes. The SDS won slightly more than 30. And there 22 was another party that won seats in the Assembly. That was the SDP, the party 23 that gathered former Communists in that period. Those were mainly the jobs we 24 carried out in 1990 and 1991. In 1992, in the spring, the conflict broke out 25 in Bosnia and in late April I was elected president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Deronjic, because I'd like to take you and ask you what were your duties and responsibilities when you were president of the Bratunac Crisis Staff? And you said you were in that capacity from I think April of 1992. Is that correct? 5 A. Correct. That's correct. In the month of April, the SDS crisis staffs 6 that we had formed in the autumn of 1991 were transformed into municipal 7 Crisis Staffs due to the hostilities, and my job was to coordinate activities 8 related to the conflicts, the clashes that were taking place in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your responsibilities include implementing policies of the government?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We implemented the decisions of the government of Republika Srpska, because in the meantime, in autumn 1991, Republika Srpska began to be established, and that was completed in January 1992, when Republika Srpska was formally established. At our level, we implemented decisions of separate agencies, mainly ministries, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Justice and other ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the exhibit marked. I will show this to you as well, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I do understand that your case manager and the registrar have agreed that the whole bundle of today would get one exhibit number. So perhaps -- I don't know where that bundle starts, whether the -- I don't take that the -- would the indictment and the plea agreement be part of the bundle as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was my understanding, Your Honour, that the indictment, the plea agreement, and the factual basis would be one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But these other exhibits would receive separate numbers. But I wasn't privy to those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend too much time on it. Madam Registrar, is it -- is the problem to make the first three documents P33, as we assigned to them, and then continue numbering? Okay. Then we have two maps on P34 and P35, and we are now at P36.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Deronjic, can be put on the screen. It should be in front of you. You mentioned in your testimony that you had been appointed to the commission on personnel and organisational issues in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And have you seen the document that is before you prior to coming into Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we now have it on our screen as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure on the coordination of this technology, Your Honour. It appears on my screen, and I assume it's on your screen, but if it's not, just please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you'll see that the name "Deronjic" appears in number 12, with the first name of "Mirodrag." Is that an error and should that be your name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is my name, and there is a mistake. My actual name is Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This appointment is dated the 9th of September, 1991, and is signed by Mr. Rajko Dukic, who is the president of the SDS Executive Board; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said, Mr. Deronjic, that you didn't start your work on this committee until 1993. Can you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I want to be completely clear and precise. I do not recall any meeting from 1991. I can't say with absolute certainty. Maybe there were meetings in 1991 that I forgot. But the reasons are very clear. In 1991, Bratunac entered a very dramatic phase in the autumn of that year. It was a stage of open conflicts in the town itself, open war. The town was full of barricades. And I was busy dealing with those problems. And in the meantime, at the state level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were also very dramatic events that resulted in a series of decisions taken by the SDS and that I was in charge of implementing. That occupied most of my time. That is why I don't think I attended a single meeting of this commission for personnel issues, although I repeat: I cannot say with absolute certainty after all these years. If that is relevant to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you also said you were a member of the Main Board of the SDS, having become a member in the summer of 1993. Can you tell the Judges your duties and responsibilities in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I named this period to the best of my recollection. I want to say again that I didn't have the opportunity to see the document by which I was appointed. I know that it was in the spring of 1993 that the party resumed its work, and I was loaned to its Main Board. I don't know the exact date. My duties were to be the political representative of the municipality and the whole region or subregion, as you wish, of Bratunac and Srebrenica, because Goran Zekic, who was my predecessor, got killed on the 8th of May, 1993 -- 1992. The duties of the members of the Main Board are prescribed by the statute of the party, and I believe they are common to all political parties. We were able to take part in the creation, in the charting of SDS policies at these sessions, to take certain decisions and to familiarise with them our membership in the field, in order for these decisions to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And finally, you said in 1996 you became a vice-president of the SDS party. Could you explain to the Judges your duties and responsibilities in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: The presidency of the SDS at that time was the highest body of the party. It consisted -- it had seven vice-presidents, as I mentioned before. And the duties of the presidency were to chart the policies and to propose certain decisions to the Main Board for consideration, after which they would be rejected or adopted, depending on the discretion of the Main Board. And then these decisions would be forwarded to state agencies that would implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were a member of the SDS party, and from the time you took your initial position in that party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
