utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I interrupt you? Have you finished with the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to show to us the second page of the translation. Because this is only partly a translation of the document. Yes. We see at the bottom of the translation, of the second page, the ERN 3587 that follows is another copy of the very same document. I noticed that you presented both 3586 and 3587, which seems to be the same document, and I wonder what would be the reason for providing us twice, I would say, approximately the same document, because there's some handwriting on 3586, that is, the number 7 on top which does not appear on the other one, whereas number 14 is -- is there any specific reason for --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: None that I'm aware of, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we then -- perhaps could you then tender one of the documents and a translation, without any reference to another similar document. That's not of great assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm glad to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, during the time that -- from the time you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, from the time you joined the SDS party and assumed your first responsibilities in it until the time you left the party positions, the highest positions which you held, did you have an opportunity to meet and discuss with SDS leaders, both on a local, municipal level, on a regional level, and on the republican level, those policies of both the SDS party and the government?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In all issues, or on all questions, the response is affirmative. I did have the opportunity in various periods, from 1990 to 1997, when I left the SDS, when I resigned my position there, to contact numerous people from the party leadership and from people at the municipal level - this is understood - also at the regional level, we met frequently and discussed all the policy matters of the party. I would also like to tell the Trial Chamber that in the formal sense, in the statutory sense, regional boards did not exist; however, we met as people who, in a certain region, had common interests and discussed certain problems related to the organisation of the party elections, all the other matters that pertained to the work and life of a party. I had the opportunity, throughout various periods, to also meet the top leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did your discussions about party policy take place both in private conversations with representatives of the SDS party from those various levels, as well as in formal sessions and meetings of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I had some kind of informal, private meetings, unless you count conversations which are usually conducted over breaks during the meetings of the Main Board or if we're meeting -- waiting for a meeting to begin in a restaurant or the different places where these meetings were held or, for example, the personnel commission, while we were preparing or waiting for everybody to assemble, then we would talk, discuss certain problems. But I never had the opportunity to visit privately at home any of the high party officials. I did not communicate with anyone in that particular manner. You could say that formally, during those meetings, I would meet people and I would acquaint them with the positions of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your capacity in the municipality of Bratunac, did you receive SDS party instructions, directives, decisions, did you analyse them and later implement them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are numerous examples of this. We convened meetings mostly in reference to different directives which we received. There were also some local needs. So then we would convene local meetings as well. There are also numerous examples when we received materials which charted the main directions of the activity of the political organs in the terrain. We would analyse them and hold meetings about them. The Prosecution is familiar with this, since they have the original minutes from those meetings, and you could see that all of this was applied, analysed, discussed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you later become a friend and associate of Dr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: This is a question to which I have already replied. It's difficult to define what it means, friendship. There was mutual respect between Mr. President, Mr. Karadzic, and myself, especially at the point in time when I joined the party presidency. I also wish to say that personal contacts or family contacts of that kind were not something that I cultivated with Mr. Karadzic, nor did I have the opportunity to meet with him in any particular environment, except at such meetings. It is true that sometimes I had the opportunity, while waiting for others to appear at certain meetings, to spend some time tete-a-tete with Mr. Karadzic or perhaps somebody else would be present as well, when we would just informally discuss certain problems. Friendship, it seems to me, is something more than that, but I allow for the possibility that my relationship with Mr. Karadzic could be interpreted as a closely knit one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in your contacts with Dr. Karadzic, did you have an opportunity to discuss with him SDS policies and governmental policies?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are numerous examples for that. I think that it is not necessary to mention them all, but we did have the opportunity to discuss certain questions, military questions, personnel questions, government policy issues, SDS policy. We did have the opportunity sometimes, just the two of us or in the company of just a few people, to discuss these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you know the accused, Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I also know Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to observe his level of influence with other members of the SDS party in the government while you were acting in your various capacities in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- the answer is affirmative. I did have the opportunity for that. I would just like to say that in 1991, I think that, except through the media, I did not personally know Mr. Krajisnik. Perhaps some meetings which I attended as the president of the municipal board of the SDS, I had the opportunity to meet him, but I don't remember having any closer contacts with him. In the course of 1992, I don't think I saw him, because my work was not linked to the work of the Assembly, and the SDS was not working. In 1993, I saw Mr. Krajisnik at meetings of the personnel commission, and I think that in a majority of those cases he attended those meetings as a member of this personnel commission. Later, as vice-president, I had the opportunity to get to know Mr. Krajisnik better, and from that period, in particular, I can provide certain views on his influence and importance in Serbian politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me take you, Mr. Deronjic, to the time when you worked in these various capacities, both on a local level and on a republican level, in the SDS. You had considerable contact, I take it, with other members of the SDS party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you able to determine the views of your colleagues in the SDS and in the government as to how they perceived Mr. Krajisnik, his role, and his influence in the party and in the government?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I say yes, although I cannot claim the right that my opinion and the opinion of my colleagues is correct. But there was an opinion that Mr. Krajisnik was a man of the highest trustworthiness in Serbian politics in general in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if I may give a conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is important at this point that the questions are very specific as to the time being referred to, because we've had a certain amount of evidence about Mr. Deronjic's positions in 1991, 1992, and 1993, but this particular line of questioning has become rather non-specific as far as time is concerned, and that ought to be made clear in the questions put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, to start with, the last question. Would you please indicate at what time you refer to when you asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will break down the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you've told us that you didn't have contact with Mr. Krajisnik in the early part of your involvement in the SDS. Nevertheless, was Mr. Krajisnik a leading figure in the SDS in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did other --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the appropriate way, we'd suggest, to ask a question of that type is to ask: What was, so far as the witness can properly give the evidence, what was Mr. Krajisnik's position in the SDS? What sort of a figure he was in the SDS? And not to ask it in terms of was Mr. Krajisnik is leading figure in the SDS, which is after all precisely what the Prosecution are attempting to establish. That's about as leading as can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say leading figure, leading question, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the perception of Mr. Krajisnik in terms of his role in the SDS party in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I will first give a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to keep objecting, but what was the perception of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the question to be what was your perception of -- is that correct? So it seems to be a misunderstanding. Mr. Deronjic, the question was translated into English to us, but perhaps not in -- no. It was said by Mr. Harmon himself. But he -- I think he misformulated the question. The question was: What was your perception of Mr. Krajisnik in terms of his role in the SDS party in 1991 and then, next question, 1992. Please proceed. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I knew Mr. Krajisnik only through the media. His role in heading the Joint Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was covered a lot in the media, so that people watched carefully broadcasts of these assembly sessions, and all the events which were reflected through the activities of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I understood Mr. Krajisnik to be one of the leading figures in the political life of Bosnia and Herzegovina and one of the leading figures in the political life of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Perhaps it is not quite the place to speak of this, but I believe that he did enjoy a certain popularity amongst the Serbian population in that period. I cannot strictly respond to the question about the policies of the SDS, because I was not familiar with his activities in the party itself, in the SDS itself, in that period. As I said, I saw him at some meetings. These were usually meetings of the Main Board, at which the presidents of the municipal boards also participated. I attended two or three such meetings, and I did not notice anything particular during that period relating to the activities in the party. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During that same period of time, are you in a position to comment about how Mr. Krajisnik was perceived by other SDS figures?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I can say that -- excuse me. I thought that we were going to have an objection. But I can say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, yes. You are going to have an objection. We're just -- whoever it was thought they might have an objection. The witness can properly give evidence about what he saw of Mr. Krajisnik's activities and Mr. Krajisnik's position in the SDS, and the witness can properly give evidence of any facts from which he draws that, but what he can't give is simply evidence of other people's perception of Mr. Krajisnik, unless it actually leads to his knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik's position. We're getting very secondhand and thirdhand here in relation to Mr. Krajisnik's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it's a perfectly appropriate question. I think this witness was in a position to associate with people in the SDS party in that time frame. He was in a position to hear what others said about Mr. Krajisnik and he was in a position to form an opinion as to what he -- how he thought Mr. Krajisnik was viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, asking questions about Mr. Deronjic's perception of how others perceived Mr. Krajisnik might easily lead to speculation. On the other hand, you are allowed to ask questions about what Mr. Deronjic observed as an expression of the perception of others. So I would rather not ask him to look in the mind of other people, but to tell us what he observed as the behaviour, also if these were spoken words of other people. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, were you in a position to hear what other people said about Mr. Krajisnik? And I'm talking about the period of time between 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber what you heard in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I've already partially responded to that question. I heard from many people that Mr. Krajisnik was a true representative of the SDS policy. Of course, I'm not quoting anybody in this sense. He was a very popular figure in that period, while he was chairing the -- or presiding over the Assembly. He was the president the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I heard from many people that he was an authority, without question, in the SDS, and that he was a close friend of Mr. Karadzic and that the two of them were the creators of the SDS policy, and that, in a certain sense, they were a tandem with the most influence in politics at the time, and in this policy. That was the prevailing opinion amongst the people who were around me at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the witness slowly moves again in the area which I would accept that it's rather speculation than personal knowledge. I mean, if he says, well, they applauded him or they said he is a good team leader or whatever direct observations conveyed to Mr. Deronjic, I think that's proper to ask, but finally we gain that the perception was that it was a team with Mr. Karadzic and in tandem with the most influence. This is too vague, so if you want to explore that part, then it should be dealt with in a more factual way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one question. I'm not sure how long we're going to proceed before we break, because we started at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break in a couple of minutes, I would say. The second break is usually a bit shorter, so you have another three to five minutes to go, and then we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in the time period when you were working on the republican level, now, did you observe Mr. Krajisnik and were you able to, based on those observations, come to any conclusions as to Mr. Krajisnik's power and authority within the SDS party and within the government? If you'd address each of those: Within the SDS party first, and then within the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if that question could be made more specific as to time, rather than give him the time period by indirect reference to his working on the republican level. It would seem more appropriate that the specific time period is given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, would you be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you, Mr. Deronjic, start working on the republican level in the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: In 1993, when I was elected to the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you now answer my question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer. I had the opportunity in that period to get better acquainted with Mr. Krajisnik and his activities. I believe that he was one of the very powerful people in Republika Srpska, which was formed in the meantime, at the state level. We considered him to be one of the key people in conducting state policy. As far as the SDS is concerned, he took part in all meetings of the Main Board. I'm not saying literally all of them. Perhaps he did have some other duties too. He did not sit at the SDS presidency, but he would sit in the first row, allocated for guests. He would participate in the debates, usually amongst the last speakers to do so. He was very suggestive in his addresses, and the Main Board would usually adopt and apply most of his proposals. Mr. Krajisnik at the time was considered to be a person who, in the operative sense, in the sense of conducting affairs of the state, he was the main person, the number-one person, and this is the opinion shared by most of the people that I knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what was his position within the party? You've just defined his position within the state. Can you make a distinction between the party and the state? And if so, can you tell us what his position was in the party.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: He was, as far as I know, a member of the same bodies of the party that I was a member of. So that was the Main Board and the personnel commission, in whose work he participated also. These are his formal posts within the party bodies. As far as his general influence on SDS policy, I believe that it extended much more broadly than that, and I believe that his influence in the SDS, his position, if I could rank it, in an informal way, was quite high, and I think that the general opinion was that he ranked right after President Karadzic by importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Am I, at this point, Your Honour, out of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not out of time. But before we adjourn, I would like to ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll adjourn, Mr. Deronjic, for almost 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic will be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher. Mr. Harmon, we had some questions put to the witness also in relation to what happened from 1993 and onwards. The Chamber wondered whether what exactly was the relevance for the indictment period?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The relevance is this, Your Honour: This witness is in a position to give his opinion as to the influence of Mr. Krajisnik. He can say, based on my conclusions in 1993, in 1994, 1995, I confirmed myself - and I haven't asked him this question yet - I confirmed what I viewed to be his position in authority and his power and authority. It's relevant only to that. It gives -- and it can be -- it should be taken only for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although the basis of his knowledge was quite different in 1993 and would allow for a -- I would say a differently based assessment compared to what his sources were in the earlier period of time. I hope that you keep that in mind when putting any further questions to the witness in this respect. And you know, retrial activity in criminal law has always been a problem. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I can say what I have to say if Your Honour had further matters to address to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, just two observations, simply to -- following the observation Your Honour has just made, we have not so far taken the position or made objections on the basis that nothing in 1993 could be relevant in the sense that time finished on the 30th or 31st of December, 1992. That would be unrealistic. But of course it is important that anything brought out in relation to a later period is brought out because it is said by the Prosecution to be directly relevant to establishing the position in the relevant time period of the indictment. But I think that was implicit in what Your Honour just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what I say -- I think it's good not to respond to every question which is outside June 1991 until December 1992. On the other hand, we should take care that we are not dwelling around too much in the adjacent periods rather than in the indictment periods, although it could certainly have some relevance. But I just wanted to ask specifically the attention of Mr. Harmon on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Our second observation, Your Honour, is a brief one. When there's reference to this witness opining, giving his opinion, this witness is not an expert witness. This witness is a witness of fact. In accordance with normal principles, when a witness gives an opinion which is in effect a convenient way of summarising what he knows factually, what he observed factually, what he can give evidence about factually, there is no objection. But if there is any question of straying into the area of opinion, as opposed to a method of conveying factual evidence, then that is outside the proper ambit of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree. It's not always easy to draw a line between the two if you would say that it's generally accepted that Zidane is a good football player, I would have hardly any reason to deny that, although, to be quite honest, I hardly ever investigated into the matter whether he really is a good football player. But the line is sometimes difficult to draw, and I think it's good that specific attention will be given to it by Mr. Harmon. We'll adjourn for -- until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you may escort the counsel of the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, we were talking about Mr. Krajisnik, and let me refocus your attention back to the period of 1991 to 1993. Do I understand your testimony to be that you only knew of Mr. Krajisnik in that time frame from the media?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. That's not how I meant it. I said that on two or three occasions, I had occasion to attend the same meetings as Mr. Krajisnik. And most of what I knew about Mr. Krajisnik was from the media. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to what you knew from the media, did you form impressions about Mr. Krajisnik's position within the SDS party as a result of your attendance of SDS meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to form a certain opinion, but those were rare occasions where I could see and hear him firsthand. It was no more than three or four times when we were together at SDS meetings. I already mentioned that he took the floor at those meetings, although I can't remember any details of his discussion or his conduct, and I can't remember any particular detail of those meetings except that he would sit in the first row, and sometimes participate in the discussion. I have no particular opinion of his role in the party except based on what I knew from the media and what I heard from my colleagues in the party, such Mr. Goran Zekic, who was our representative, and we talked about Mr. Krajisnik, and his opinion was that Mr. Krajisnik was one of the undisputed authorities in the SDS and in the policies carried out by that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Zekic, Goran Zekic, was a political figure from Srebrenica, the municipality that was adjacent to Bratunac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Zekic was on the Main Board of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct. I believe from the foundation of the SDS, he was member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He was also a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he in frequent contact with the leadership at the republican level, based on those positions that he held? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He was in frequent contact with the leadership because he held the greatest number of positions representing our region in the topmost republican and other authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you and Mr. Zekic have frequent contact and conversations during the period of time of 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We talked very often, even privately, because we were friends, and formally, at meetings, because he would often bring materials from the sessions of the Main Board, and he took it upon himself to forward these materials to our board, our council in Bratunac. And he often participated in the work of our board in Bratunac, and he would convey to us the instructions and decisions of the Main Board, and interpreted them for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And would he also discuss with you, in a way that you understood to be less formal, his observations about what was happening at the higher levels in the SDS party and in the government?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zekic and I were friends. We had numerous occasions to discuss informally the policies of the Serbian Democratic Party, that is, to say my answer is affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did he discuss with you the various personalities, including Mr. Krajisnik, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Certainly. We talked about all the prominent personalities featuring in SDS politics. I don't remember the places and times when we discussed particular individuals, but it was normal for us to discuss the leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zekic express to you his view of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The area that was discussed before the break, the question of opinion, this is an even more extreme case of something which is potentially highly objectionable. Mr. Zekic won't be giving his opinion because he's no longer alive. But given that if we're talking about opinion, crossing that line -- we acknowledge a slightly difficult line, but if we're talking about opinion crossing that line, even if Mr. Zekic himself were here giving his evidence, his simple opinion, except as a way of conveying observations, would not be admissible evidence. So even more strongly it follows that this witness's report of what Mr. Zekic might have expressed to him as an opinion is clearly objectionable. So this is an advance of the answer, but the question seems at the moment to lead on to a very clear danger, of the answer crossing that illegitimate line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I think it is a fair question to ask. I think the Court can give the answer whatever way it deems appropriate. It's -- for example, Your Honour, I think it's fairly common in discussing, in organisational terms, views about who has -- who is, for example, the leader or the most powerful person or give characterisations as to positions. It happens every day. And that's what I'm asking this witness, and Your Honours can take the answer and give it whatever weight you deem appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Mr. Harmon, you may ask what the witness heard from Mr. Zekic, and you should keep full control over whenever we deviate from what someone could observe and when it comes to speculation and opinion, in the true sense of the word. Not every assessment is necessarily opinion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you hear from Mr. Zekic in respect of Mr. Krajisnik's position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'll be brief in my answer. I can't remember any relevant opinion expressed by Mr. Zekic about Mr. Krajisnik. I only said that it was the general opinion that Mr. Krajisnik was a very powerful man. I cannot recall a single particular description or reference by Mr. Zekic in respect of Mr. Krajisnik, and I agree that I would go into speculation if I attempted to quote something like that. And I think that would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, Mr. Deronjic, to July of 1991. You have informed us that you attended some meetings during that period of time, some SDS meetings, and I'd like to direct your attention to a meeting that was held on the 12th of July, in Sarajevo, a session of the SDS Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have that next exhibit marked and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P37.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could -- yes, please. If you could show the B/C/S version to Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, have you seen that document prior to coming into the courtroom today to testify?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, I have had occasion to see this document. It was a couple of days ago, when I was preparing to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you attend this particular session of the SDS Assembly on the 12th of July, 1991, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can see from this document that I attended this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in that session of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik was indeed lauded as being one of the eminent political figures from the ranks of the Bosnian Serb people. Do you recall Mr. Karadzic lauding him that way? And I can direct your attention to page 14. Sorry. We are trying to coordinate the technical aspects of this. Does the English version of this appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. If the Prosecution are attempting to elicit evidence that Mr. Krajisnik was lauded as an influential figure at a particular meeting, to bring up a minute which shows it recorded that that happened and then to ask him whether that happened is absolutely not the right way of doing it. What the Prosecution must, with respect, we submit, do in those circumstances is ask the witness whether he was at that meeting; ask the witness whether he recalls Mr. Krajisnik being at that meeting, or they can do those questions the other way round; and then in a non-leading way, see whether the witness gives that evidence, but not point him to the record of exactly what it is that they're attempting to elicit from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was trying to direct the witness's attention to this particular element. Mr. Deronjic has said he attended this meeting. He has had an opportunity to review this transcript. I can ask him six questions to get to this point. My time is limited with this witness. This is merely illustrative for purposes of Mr. Deronjic's prior testimony. If the Court wants, I can take this examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we find a way in between? I would say to some extent I agree that to say was he lauded and then present a piece of paper in which it says he was lauded is then perhaps -- as has happened also, and that of course could be a consequence, just ask him is this a report of this meeting and then have that report in evidence which, of course, would not -- of course you could cross-examine him on it. That would save a lot of time, perhaps one or two questions, although coming to the point quickly, and if the answer could be then confirmed if you find at least the answer in accordance with what we find in this paper, to have that confirmed, that might be the appropriate way of doing it. But putting the text in front of him and say: Isn't is true that this is what happened? Might be a bit too time-saving, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm happy to withdraw the question. This will be an exhibit in evidence, and we can -- it will stand on its own. I will withdraw the question and I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, at this meeting was there an election for the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This meeting elected the Main Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to July the 12th, 1991, was there already a main -- an SDS Main Board in existence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't remember. I wasn't a member then, and I wouldn't go into guesswork. I suppose there was. I can't say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll -- were you a candidate for the SDS Main Board on this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on that particular occasion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you a candidate from the region -- the Birac region?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recall how many votes you received?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: A few. I don't remember the exact number. I believe it was something like eight. I don't remember the number. I knew I didn't pass, but I saw here in one of the documents that it was eight votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was elected from the SDS Birac region to the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If you want me to tell you from my memory, I could only remember Mr. Zekic, Mr. Dukic, and I don't think I remember anyone else, save perhaps for Mr. Mijatovic, from Zvornik. But here in this file there is a document where we could see that. I'm not sure who was elected as representative from Birac. I know that Zekic and Dukic were certainly members of the Main Board, and Mijatovic, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will direct the Court's attention to page 88 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, do you have in front of you, toward the end of that document, the results from the Birac region? If not, there's no reason to look through it now.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I have it on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I have the results on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you confirm those were the results that took place at this session? If not, we'll move on to another area, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Mr. Dukic and Mr. Zekic were elected members of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Mr. Krajisnik was also elected to the Main Board on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that Mr. Krajisnik was elected to the Main Board at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can direct Your Honours' attention to pages 92 and 93 in the English version, first showing apparently 92 in the highlighted section, indicates that the number of people who were elected to the Main Board. And if we could go to the next page, the identities of the people who were elected are listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. As I indicated at the beginning of this session, the Chamber would exercise its supervision or control of the examination perhaps more profoundly than usual. May I ask you one question: You said you didn't know whether there was any Main Board before you were elected. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, Your Excellency, I can't remember with absolute certainty, and I would hate to give a wrong answer. I think there was, but I'm not absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us just a couple of minutes ago that Mr. Zekic was member of the Main Board on from the SDS to be founded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. Maybe I misspoke. He could not have been a member of the Main Board of a party that was only to be established. After its establishment, yes, I think he was a member of its Main Board. In other words, I think he was a member of the Main Board since -- from the day when the Main Board came into existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were a member of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the Main Board from 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just wondered whether there was any contradiction between it. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while this list of the 45 people who were elected to the Main Board on this occasion are before you, we will be hearing testimony about a number of personalities in the upcoming testimony, and if I can direct Your Honours' attention to some of those names so you can familiarise yourself with these names before the testimony. Obviously, number 1, number 35, number 36, number 31, and numbers 8 and 9. Those are names that you will be hearing in the testimony of Mr. Deronjic. You may hear some of the other names as well, but I wanted to direct your attention to those particular names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go backwards in time, Mr. Deronjic. I would like to go backwards in time to a meeting in approximately April of 1991, in Sarajevo, that you attended. Do you know the meeting I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my interview, I referred to that meeting that took place in the spring. I suppose it was April 1991. Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of meeting it was, what the subject matter was and who attended.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It was a meeting of the Main Board, in its enlarged composition, including presidents of municipal boards, and it was attended by the highest party leadership in that period. I wasn't able to remember the exact date of that meeting when I gave the interview, and I'm still unable to remember it. Nor can I remember the exact venue. What I do remember is that those meetings that we held in Sarajevo, some of which I attended, took place in the Holiday Inn Hotel on several occasions, plus some in the Villa Srbijanka, in the Ilidza neighbour of Sarajevo. The meeting discussed the usual topics that were common to the political life of Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as the topical events in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Yugoslavia, and their repercussions on Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Karadzic would give an introductory contribution, which I don't remember in its entirety, but I quoted certain parts in my interview. I don't remember anyone else who spoke at that meeting. But I remember that meeting because I heard then for the first time one sentence that marked a new thrust in the policy of the SDS; namely, on that occasion, Mr. Karadzic said publicly that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Yugoslavia is such that if the federal Yugoslavia no longer exists, and it obviously doesn't, then the only option open to the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the creation of Greater Serbia. This is not a quotation, but it is the sense of what he said. I remember that sentence that he uttered, and I remembered it as an idea that I myself used later at some meetings at the local level. At that particular moment, however, it didn't mean anything much to me, because it is well-known that, in practice, politicians sometimes 23 make some strong statement that is intended either to instil fear in or 24 surprise political enemies. However,when I thought about that meeting later,I came to the conclusion that the spring of 1991 marked a new chapter in the life of the SDS party and an abandonment of its previous principles, whereas the basic principle at the time of the foundation of the SDS was the preservation of the federal Yugoslavia. After that meeting, I had occasion to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, Mr. Deronjic. I want to ask you some questions about this. First of all, you said that there were presidents of SDS municipal boards and deputies of the Joint Assembly. Can you identify those people by name that you recall as being present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I know that those sessions were always attended by all those who were invited, with few exceptions of people who were for some reason unable to attend. I enumerated people whom I knew to have been presidents of municipal boards at the time, like myself, Mr. Zekic, Mr. Brano Grujic, Mr. Dukic. Those were men from the neighbouring municipalities whom I knew personally. I presume that they were at that meeting. What I know for sure is that I saw there certain persons who later attended an informal conversation, Mrs. Hrvacanin, Mr. Zekic, and some others. I was at that meeting myself. That's why I remember it. And of course, those meetings were also attended by the highest state officials, including members of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, although of course I can't say with 100 per cent certainty that they were there. I don’t really remember all these details. Mr. Krajisnik, and so on. As far as I can remember, those were the attendees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you expand on the shift in the policy and what you perceive the importance of that shift to be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I have already said before this Honourable Court that my thoughts about the importance of that moment only came later, when I focussed in a more serious way on all that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in light of my own fate, of course. As I see things today, that meeting was a consequence of various developments in the former Yugoslavia, and most importantly, it was a consequence in the shift of policy of Serbia and Croatia towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. Because at that time a meeting was held, of which I know only today, that is, the secret meeting between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman in the spring of 1991, and as far as I know today, that was when the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina was agreed between them. 12 I view this meeting in this context. However, it also had other political 13 contexts.First and foremost, the conduct of the SDA and the Muslim leadership 14 in Bosnia and Herzegovina.I wish to remind you that in the spring of 1991,SDA came forward with a concept of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and proposed it to the Republican Assembly in the form of a declaration. Then we have the well-known events in Croatia. That is the time when those well-known decisions were made by the Serbian people in Croatia. The Serbian Krajina, for instance, took the decision to annex their area to Serbia. So these are the events that I know of today, and I know that discussions took place in that context, and I believe it was the period when a certain shift occurred in the policy of the SDS. And I link that to another event as well. In the spring of 1991, there was this famous rally in Belgrade, a rally of opposition parties against Slobodan Milosevic, and we know the epilogue of that event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you. This seems more comments on political events rather than testimony on facts. I wouldn't say that it's totally irrelevant, but it is a bit too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours will see that it's important to put the context in to understand the later events, and that's why I was giving Mr. Deronjic some liberty in terms of his answer. I will proceed, however, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, following this meeting where Mr. Karadzic gave the -- made these certain remarks, did you have the opportunity to attend a smaller meeting? And if so, can you tell us who attended that meeting and where it took place.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attended a minor meeting. This was -- the term "meeting" is used in a formal sense, but the meeting was actually held in a restaurant. And I said that as far as I could recall, it was held at the Nacional restaurant in Sarajevo. I remember that we were sitting there. Mr. Zekic, myself, Mr. Karadzic, Ostojic, Mrs. Hrvacanin. So this was the company present. I remember that Mr. Karadzic continued --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt again because it's important that the Judges understand who these people are. When you say Mr. Ostojic, you mean Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I'm thinking of Mr. Velibor Ostojic. In that period, as far as I know, he was the vice-president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what other positions did he hold thereafter? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: For a while after that, he was the president of the SDS Executive Board, and afterwards, for a certain period, he was the minister of information in the government of Republika Srpska, and the deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said Goran Zekic. Can you outline briefly for the Judges the positions that he held.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I think that we mentioned it. He was the president of the SDS municipal board, deputy in the common -- the Joint Assembly, and later in the Assembly of Republika Srpska, member of the Main Board of the SDS. I think that he also had some kind of function in the legislative commission, the legislative committee of the Assembly. I think he was perhaps the president of the legislative commission, but I think this is something that he told me. I never saw any document indicating this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the final participant you mentioned was Slobodanka Hrvacanin. What position did she hold, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: She was a member of the Main Board and she was the president of the municipal board in Zenica, of the SDS municipal board in Zenica. I know little about her, because I didn't really see her that much in the ranks of the SDS later on, but she was somebody who was well known during the initial activities of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, then, what took place at that restaurant meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic briefly talked about the political developments. Then he said something during the discussion, which to me seemed important - I remembered it - that it was agreed that Bosnia would be divided. That was the essence of that one sentence of his. He also made an additional comment to the effect that those who were afraid to take part in that should not take part in that. That was the comment. I know that he discussed some details with Mrs. Hrvacanin relating to the position of Serbs in Zenica. I don't recall all the particulars. This was a long time ago, and these things that I do remember, I am saying that they're true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in your mind, Mr. Deronjic, were those comments significant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you? I see that the Defence is a bit at unrest for a reason they can't see at a distance. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, yes. We were actually just asking ourselves, but then, as a preliminary to asking very directly through the Tribunal: What it is that the witness has in front of him? Because he has a written file and written papers in front of him and we would ask what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can tell you it's the previous exhibit. It's the minutes from the session of the Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't see anything because the screen is just in front of it. I take it that who was the better eyes is another question. Perhaps in order to avoid whatever confusion, could you please close whatever is in front of you. If it is an exhibit that still should be returned to the registrar, that could be done now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. It appears there's nothing sinister, as it turns out, but it is important for us to check. We would ask, and I think that's implicit in what Your Honour has just said, we would ask, because the witness did bring some sort of file with him which appears to be closed, but we would ask that he only ever has in front of him, unless it's specifically drawn to the attention of the Tribunal, the specific document which he's being asked by counsel or the Tribunal to look at at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the parties will keep an eye on it, because I can't see it. But you're instructed not to have any paper in front of you. Of course, I follow the eyes of the witness and I did not see him consult anything in front of him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the record reflect, just so it's perfectly clear that what was in front of Mr. Deronjic was the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it was then taken by the usher and given to the registrar, and I can see with my own eyes that it was the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, again, my question to you is: What was the significance of Mr. Karadzic's remarks in that small restaurant meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I can state with certainty today that this was a period in which the party had a different position. At that time, of course, there were comments about the situation, but I understood that this remark about the division of Bosnia was stated by Mr. Karadzic in a confidential manner, and I did not really comment much on that at the local level. This was just a remark that I made that this was something new in the political practice of the SDS. But my true information about those events actually dates back from a later period when I analysed it a little bit more and reached certain conclusions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the division -- was the proposition that Bosnia would be divided included in the SDS party programme at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. The SDS stood for the policy of the preservation of Yugoslavia in the form it existed in, as a federal community of republics. Officially, that concept was valid until the fall of 1991, when Republika Srpska was formed, openly, which at least formally, meant the 10 abandonment of the SDS programme on the integrity or unity of Bosnia, and 11 the unity of Yugoslavia as a joint state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, following these particular meetings in April of 1991, did you receive instructions to prepare maps in respect of the ethnic composition of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In a certain period in 1991, we received orders from the party, from the party leadership, to prepare maps of our municipalities with an as precise as possible representation of the ethnic structure in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say: "Ethnic structure within the municipality," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It was necessary, according to the instructions, to indicate by colour settlements and their ethnic composition. Villages and towns which were populated by Serbs were marked by the colour blue, and those inhabited by Muslims were marked in green, while Croats in Bratunac only numbered about five or six, so we did not take those figures into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you prepare those maps?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did make such a map of the Bratunac municipality, and we passed it on to the republican party leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you recall to whom that map was sent? When you say: "The republican leadership," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: This had to be given to the president or the presidency of the party. I really don't know how the party leadership functioned at that time, but there were technical teams within the party which carried out such tasks. In the technical sense, they would send us instructions and then what we did would send that back to the technical department of the party, and then they would make sure that that was given to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I ask you to have a look at the clock. It's one minute off from a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know why, Mr. Deronjic, those maps were prepared?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I concluded, and this conclusion was formed later, and it has to do with the founding of Serbian Autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Because in the coming period, one of the main activities of the SDS was to form Serbian autonomous regions. In order to form those regions, I don't know exactly, but they probably used these maps. They also used legal and constitutional options in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the form of association of municipalities for some kind of common purpose. Later, these municipalities were verified as constitutive parts. Those regions were identified as constitutive parts of the territory of Republika Srpska. This was done at an Assembly session in October. And then later, it became clear that they were actually formed with that intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've concluded, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Deronjic, it's time for us to stop. I'll ask the security to escort you out of the courtroom. We'll start again tomorrow morning at 9.00, for your information, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 for your information. Same courtroom. I take it that there's nothing urgent to be discussed at this very moment. I see only nodding no. Therefore, we adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
